summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since May 1998 and sex between women was never criminalised; the age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation. That legality is not backed by protection. No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the country's first anti-discrimination statute, adopted in July 2022, dropped both grounds and retains only "sex". A monitoring review covering 2024 finds the law only partially aligned with international standards, and a legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records barriers and gaps for gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including situations where the written law protects but practice does not.

Police keep a register of LGBTIQ people, introduced in 2016; a separate account dates a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons to 2017. A regional review covering 2024 describes officers luring LGBT people into staged meetings in order to enter them in the database, harvesting contact lists from their social media and extracting money, with more than ten such cases recorded in the Sughd region.

Raids carried out in 2022 and 2023 produced forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges. Documented police conduct includes ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion. In 2024 a regional monitoring organisation recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people, among them arbitrary arrest, blackmail and extortion. That is a count of cases an organisation was able to record, not a rate, and no denominator accompanies it.

Gender-affirming medical services are not available inside Tajikistan, and a trans visitor cannot obtain hormone therapy or surgical care locally. Trans people who can travel go abroad to transition. Most doctors in the country have no expertise in the treatments involved. A 2024 regional study of trans people's access to medical services, covering HIV prevention and treatment and hormone therapy, includes a Tajikistan country coordinator and carries guidance for trans migrants. Patients report disrespectful treatment from medical staff.

Legal gender change is blocked in practice. Tajik law permits reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official papers for that purpose, so a trans visitor has no route to correcting a local record.

No relationship-recognition framework exists. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status cannot have it recognised, and same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections that attach to marriage.

Public expression of support for LGBT people is effectively suppressed, and public attitudes have been described as entirely negative. Homophobic and transphobic statements by politicians form part of ordinary political life, and the country's senior religious authority, the Supreme Mufti Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a disaster, condemned states that legalise same-sex marriage and spoken against rights activists and anti-discrimination legislation.

Where a person is known or suspected of being LGBT, disclosure brings physical and psychological abuse, including from police. Reporting from 2013, fifteen years after decriminalisation, found very little tolerance and described the community as one of the most closed in society.
tangentialFactors:
The deterioration of the wider political environment forms the background to the policing the sources document. In 2016 opposition leaders were sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned and a referendum extending presidential rule passed, which left few avenues of independent recourse open when the police register was established.

The 2024 study of trans people's access to medical services is regional in scope, covering several countries of the same region; its national findings are not separately itemised in the published material, and the Tajikistan content consists of the participation of a country coordinator. The 2020 legislative analysis is comparative in design and rests on a questionnaire completed by local partners, so the obstacles it records are reported rather than adjudicated.
localsOnly:
Residents who need gender-affirming care must leave the country. No such services are provided inside Tajikistan, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments trans patients need. A trans-focused NGO has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol and uses it to educate endocrinologists.

Changing legal gender requires a diagnosis of transsexualism, with surgery required for trans women and not for trans men, decided by commissions of three psychiatrists working case by case without a regulating procedure; activists say bribes are often necessary. Medical institutions issue no official documents for the purpose, and between three and six people have completed a change of legal gender.

Two LGBT organisations operate anonymously, one working only on trans issues and one on general LGBT issues. Neither has access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, which rules out advocacy at state level.

Trans and LGB patients report disrespectful treatment by medical staff, and some psychologists and doctors offer methods presented as cures that treat homosexuality as an addiction on the model of alcoholism or drug dependence.

Same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to married heterosexual couples, and no framework recognises the relationship.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prison conditions and placement of trans detainees are unresolved. A human-rights review published in 2025 records detention material concerning opposition figures and deportees only; no conditions or placement of trans detainees are documented.

Accounts differ on when police began registering LGBT people: one dates the register to 2016, another to a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons in 2017. Neither describes how the register is maintained or who may be entered in it.

Recorded violation counts depend on what a monitoring organisation can document from a community that reports anonymously. The 27 cases recorded for 2024 are not a prevalence measure, and no denominator is available.

No findings are available on LGBT minors, education-sector policies or school environments. Visa, entry and border-screening rules bearing on trans travellers to Tajikistan are not documented in the sources available.
